title: Paper 1: Applications of Mathematical Knowledge
target_note: 7+ candidates should finish with time to spare and get 15 or more.

questions.stem_html:
The equation

4x − 2x+3 + 15 = 0

has exactly two real solutions. The sum of these two solutions is
questions.solution_html:
Write t = 2x. Then 4x = t2 and 2x+3 = 8t, so the equation is t2 − 8t + 15 = 0, i.e. (t − 3)(t − 5) = 0.

So 2x = 3 or 2x = 5, giving x = log2 3 and x = log2 5. Both are valid because both values of t are positive.

Sum = log2 3 + log2 5 = log2 15.

traps.A: 3 is log₂ 8: this is what you get by adding the two values of t (3 + 5 = 8) and then taking the log. The sum of logs is the log of the product, not of the sum.
traps.B: 8 is the sum of the t-values, not the x-values.
traps.D: 15 is the product of the t-values; the question asks for the sum of the solutions x.
traps.E: log₂ 2 = 1 would need the two values of t to multiply to 2.
traps.F: Adds an extra spurious term.

questions.stem_html:
How many integers n satisfy both of the inequalities

n2 − 30n + 200 < 0   and   n2 > 18n − 65 ?
questions.solution_html:
First inequality: (n − 10)(n − 20) < 0, so 10 < n < 20. That gives the integers 11 to 19 inclusive (nine of them).

Second inequality: n2 − 18n + 65 > 0, i.e. (n − 5)(n − 13) > 0, so n < 5 or n > 13.

Both: 13 < n < 20, i.e. n = 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19. That is 6 integers.

traps.A: 5 comes from miscounting 14–19 or from using n ≥ 15.
traps.C: 7 comes from including n = 13, but 13 makes the second expression equal to zero, and the inequality is strict.
traps.E: 9 is the count from the first inequality alone.
traps.F: 15 comes from taking the inequalities as 'or' rather than 'and'.

questions.stem_html:
The polynomial p(x) = x3 + ax + b, where a and b are constants, has (x − 2)2 as a factor.

What is the value of b?
questions.solution_html:
(x − 2)2 is a factor, so x = 2 is a repeated root. A repeated root of a polynomial is also a root of its derivative, so p(2) = 0 and p′(2) = 0.

p′(x) = 3x2 + a, so p′(2) = 12 + a = 0, giving a = −12.

p(2) = 8 + 2a + b = 8 − 24 + b = 0, so b = 16.

Check: x3 − 12x + 16 = (x − 2)2(x + 4). Expanding the right-hand side confirms it.

If you only used p(2) = 0 you get one equation in two unknowns and cannot finish. The "repeated" is the whole question.

traps.A: −16 comes from a sign slip in 8 + 2a + b = 0.
traps.B: −8 comes from forgetting the 2a term entirely (8 + b = 0).
traps.C: 4 comes from taking (x − 2) as a factor with the third root also 2, giving (x−2)³ which has no x term matching the form given.
traps.D: 8 comes from using p′(2) = 0 correctly but then substituting a = +12.
traps.F: 24 comes from 8 + 2a + b = 0 with a = +8 (from 12 − a = 0 sign error).

questions.stem_html:
The equation

x2 + (k − 3)x + k = 0

has two distinct real roots, both of which are positive.

The complete set of possible values of k is
questions.solution_html:
Three conditions, all needed.

Distinct real roots: (k − 3)2 − 4k > 0, i.e. k2 − 10k + 9 > 0, i.e. (k − 1)(k − 9) > 0, so k < 1 or k > 9.

Both positive means the sum is positive and the product is positive. Sum of roots = −(k − 3) = 3 − k > 0, so k < 3. Product = k > 0.

Intersecting: 0 < k < 3 with (k < 1 or k > 9) gives 0 < k < 1.

Sanity check with k = ½: x2 − 2.5x + 0.5 = 0 has discriminant 6.25 − 2 > 0 and roots that are both positive. ✓

traps.A: This is the discriminant condition alone; it ignores that the roots must be positive.
traps.B: k > 9 gives real roots but their sum 3 − k is negative, so both roots are negative.
traps.C: This is the 'both positive' condition alone (Vieta), ignoring the discriminant.
traps.E: Ignores the product condition: k ≤ 0 gives a non-positive root.
traps.F: For 1 < k < 3 the discriminant is negative: no real roots.

questions.stem_html:
A sequence is defined by x1 = 3 and

xn+1 = 11 − xn  for n ≥ 1.

What is the sum of the first 2026 terms of the sequence?
questions.solution_html:
Compute the first few terms: x1 = 3, x2 = 1/(1 − 3) = −½, x3 = 1/(1 + ½) = ⅔, x4 = 1/(1 − ⅔) = 3.

So the sequence has period 3: 3, −½, ⅔, 3, −½, ⅔, …

One full cycle sums to 3 − ½ + ⅔ = 196.

2026 = 3 × 675 + 1, so the first 2026 terms are 675 complete cycles followed by one more term, which is x2026 = x1 = 3.

Sum = 675 × 196 + 3 = 128256 + 3 = 42752 + 62 = 42812.

traps.A: 4274/2 adds x₂ = −½ as the leftover term instead of x₁.
traps.B: 4275/2 is 675 cycles with the 2026th term forgotten.
traps.C: 6413/3 adds x₃ = ⅔ as the leftover term.
traps.D: 4287/2 comes from adding 6 (two extra terms) instead of 3.
traps.F: 2026 assumes every term is 1.

questions.stem_html:
What is the coefficient of x3 in the expansion of

(1 + x + x2)5 ?
questions.solution_html:
Treat it as (1 + u)5 with u = x + x2. The general term is 5Cr ur.

x3 can arise only from r = 2 and r = 3 (r = 1 tops out at x2; r ≥ 4 starts at x4).

r = 2: (x + x2)2 = x2 + 2x3 + x4, coefficient of x3 is 2. Contribution 10 × 2 = 20.

r = 3: (x + x2)3 starts x3 + …, coefficient 1. Contribution 10 × 1 = 10.

Total 30.

traps.C: 25 comes from ⁵C₂ + ⁵C₃ with the inner coefficient of 2 forgotten (10 + 10 = 20) plus a miscount; there is no route to 25.
traps.F: 60 uses 3! ordering incorrectly.

questions.stem_html:
The circle C has equation x2 + y2 − 6x + 4y = 12.

The line y = x + c is a tangent to C.

What is the product of the possible values of c?
questions.solution_html:
Complete the square: (x − 3)2 + (y + 2)2 = 12 + 9 + 4 = 25. Centre (3, −2), radius 5.

The line is x − y + c = 0. It is a tangent when the distance from the centre equals the radius:

|3 − (−2) + c|√2 = 5, so |5 + c| = 5√2.

Hence c = −5 + 5√2 or c = −5 − 5√2.

Product = (−5)2 − (5√2)2 = 25 − 50 = −25.

Alternative: substitute y = x + c into the circle and set the discriminant to zero. You get 2x² + (2c − 2)x + (c² + 4c − 12) = 0, discriminant zero gives c² + 10c − 25 = 0, whose product of roots is −25 by Vieta. Same answer, more algebra.

traps.A: −50 is (5√2)² with the sign flipped and the 25 dropped.
traps.C: −10 is the sum of the two values of c, not the product.
traps.D: 25 is r² and also what you get from a sign error in the difference of two squares.
traps.F: This is one of the values of c, not their product.

questions.stem_html:
How many solutions does the equation

2 sin2(2x) + 3 cos(2x) = 0

have in the interval 0° ≤ x < 360° ?
questions.solution_html:
Let u = 2x, so 0° ≤ u < 720°.

Use sin2u = 1 − cos2u: 2 − 2cos2u + 3cosu = 0, i.e. 2cos2u − 3cosu − 2 = 0, i.e. (2cosu + 1)(cosu − 2) = 0.

cosu = 2 is impossible. cosu = −½ gives u = 120°, 240°, 480°, 600° in [0, 720°).

Each u gives exactly one x = u/2, so there are 4 solutions: x = 60°, 120°, 240°, 300°.

traps.A: 0 comes from wrongly rejecting cos u = −½ as well as cos u = 2.
traps.B: 2 counts solutions of cos u = −½ in [0°, 360°) only, forgetting that 2x runs to 720°.
traps.D: 6 comes from adding two spurious solutions from cos u = 2.
traps.E: 8 comes from doubling the correct count of 4 'because of the 2x', but the doubling is already accounted for by extending the u-interval.
traps.F: 12 has no valid derivation.

questions.stem_html:
In triangle ABC, AB = 6, BC = 4 and angle BAC = 30°.

There are two possible triangles. What is the difference between the two possible lengths of AC?
questions.diagram_svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" width="330" role="img" aria-label="Triangle ABC with AB = 6, BC = 4, angle at A 30 degrees, two possible positions for C">
  <g fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.6">
   <line x1="40" y1="160" x2="190" y2="160"/>
   <line x1="40" y1="160" x2="230" y2="50" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke="#777"/>
   <line x1="190" y1="160" x2="95.2" y2="128.2"/>
   <line x1="190" y1="160" x2="209.7" y2="62"/>
   <path d="M 70 160 A 30 30 0 0 0 66 145"/>
  </g>
  <g font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic" font-size="14" fill="#111">
   <text x="28" y="176">A</text><text x="186" y="178">B</text>
   <text x="212" y="58">C</text><text x="80" y="122">C′</text>
  </g>
  <g font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#111">
   <text x="108" y="178">6</text><text x="207" y="118">4</text><text x="128" y="138">4</text><text x="74" y="155">30°</text>
  </g></svg>
questions.solution_html:
Let AC = b. Cosine rule on angle A: BC2 = AB2 + AC2 − 2·AB·AC·cos 30°.

16 = 36 + b2 − 12b·(√3/2), so b2 − 6√3b + 20 = 0.

b = 6√3 ± √108 − 802 = 6√3 ± 2√72 = 3√3 ± √7.

Both are positive (3√3 ≈ 5.2 > √7 ≈ 2.6), which is why there are two triangles: this is the angle–side–side ambiguous case.

Difference = (3√3 + √7) − (3√3 − √7) = 2√7.

traps.B: 2√3 comes from misreading √108 as 6 rather than 6√3 in the discriminant.
traps.C: √7 is half the difference: the ± term itself, before you subtract the two roots.
traps.D: 4 is the length BC, not a difference.
traps.E: 6√3 is the sum of the two possible lengths, not the difference.
traps.F: This is the smaller of the two lengths, not the difference.

questions.stem_html:
A sector of a circle has radius r and angle θ radians. Its perimeter is 20 and its area is 24.

What is the sum of all possible values of θ?
questions.solution_html:
Perimeter: 2r + rθ = 20. Area: ½r2θ = 24, so rθ = 48/r.

Substitute: 2r + 48/r = 20, so 2r2 − 20r + 48 = 0, i.e. r2 − 10r + 24 = 0, i.e. (r − 4)(r − 6) = 0.

r = 4 gives θ = 48/16 = 3. r = 6 gives θ = 48/36 = 4/3.

Both are valid angles (less than 2π). Sum = 3 + 4/3 = 13/3.

traps.A: 4/3 is one of the two values only.
traps.B: 3 is one of the two values only.
traps.C: 10/3 comes from 2 + 4/3 (an arithmetic slip on r = 4).
traps.E: 10 is the sum of the possible radii, not the angles.
traps.F: 20/3 doubles the correct answer.

questions.stem_html:
Find the exact solution of

32x+1 = 5x−1.

(log means log10.)
questions.solution_html:
Take logs of both sides: (2x + 1) log 3 = (x − 1) log 5.

2x log 3 + log 3 = x log 5 − log 5.

x(2 log 3 − log 5) = −log 5 − log 3 = −log 15.

x = −log 152 log 3 − log 5 = log 15log 5 − 2 log 3.

Sanity: 2 log 3 = log 9 < log 5? No, log 9 > log 5, so the denominator log 5 − 2 log 3 is negative and x is negative. Check with the original: for negative x the left side 32x+1 is small and the right side 5x−1 is small; plausible. ✓

traps.B: This is the correct expression with the sign lost when moving −log 15 across; it equals −x.
traps.C: Denominator sign error: the log 5 term moved to the left without changing sign.
traps.D: Mixed up which logs are multiplied by x and which are constants.
traps.E: Dropped the factor of 2 on log 3 and mishandled signs.
traps.F: Treated log 3 − log 5 as the constant term instead of −(log 3 + log 5).

questions.topic: Tangents to a curve from an external point
questions.stem_html:
Two distinct tangents to the curve y = x2 pass through the point (1, −3).

What is the product of the gradients of these two tangents?
questions.solution_html:
The tangent at (a, a2) has gradient 2a and equation y = 2ax − a2.

It passes through (1, −3): −3 = 2a − a2, so a2 − 2a − 3 = 0, i.e. (a − 3)(a + 1) = 0.

So a = 3 or a = −1. Gradients are 6 and −2.

Product = −12.

Fast route: gradients are 2a₁ and 2a₂, so the product is 4a₁a₂ = 4 × (−3) = −12 by Vieta, without finding the roots.

traps.B: −6 is the product of the a-values times 2, not times 4.
traps.C: −3 is the product of the a-values (points of tangency), not the gradients.
traps.D: 2 is the sum of the a-values.
traps.E: 4 is the sum of the gradients.
traps.F: 12 has the sign wrong.

questions.topic: Stationary points & the nature of turning points
questions.stem_html:
The curve y = 2x3 − 9x2 + 12x + k has a local maximum that lies on the x-axis.

What is the value of k?
questions.solution_html:
dydx = 6x2 − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2). Stationary points at x = 1 and x = 2.

d2ydx2 = 12x − 18: negative at x = 1 (maximum), positive at x = 2 (minimum).

The maximum is at x = 1 with y = 2 − 9 + 12 + k = 5 + k. On the axis means 5 + k = 0, so k = −5.

traps.B: −4 puts the minimum (x = 2, where y = 4 + k) on the axis, not the maximum.
traps.D: 1 comes from a sign error in 2 − 9 + 12.
traps.E: 4 puts the minimum on the axis with a sign flip.
traps.F: 5 is 5 + k = 0 solved with the wrong sign.

questions.topic: Area between a curve and the x-axis
questions.stem_html:
The curve y = x3 − 4x2 + 3x crosses the x-axis at x = 0, 1 and 3, as shown.

What is the total area of the regions enclosed between the curve and the x-axis for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3?
questions.solution_html:
The curve is above the axis on (0, 1) and below it on (1, 3), so integrate the two pieces separately and add their sizes.

Antiderivative: F(x) = x44 − 4x33 + 3x22.

F(1) − F(0) = ¼ − 4/3 + 3/2 = 3 − 16 + 1812 = 512.

F(3) − F(1) = (81/4 − 36 + 27/2) − 5/12 = −9/4 − 5/12 = −3212 = −83.

Area = 512 + 83 = 512 + 3212 = 3712.

traps.A: 5/12 is the area of the first region only.
traps.B: 9/4 is the size of the single definite integral from 0 to 3 (which is −9/4): the two regions partly cancel.
traps.C: 8/3 is the area of the second region only.
traps.E: −9/4 is the definite integral from 0 to 3, not an area.
traps.F: 27/4 comes from an arithmetic slip in F(3).

questions.stem_html:
PA and PB are tangents from an external point P to a circle with centre O. Angle APB = 2θ.

The point C lies on the minor arc AB, as shown.

What is angle ACB?
questions.diagram_svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 240" width="340" role="img" aria-label="Circle centre O with tangents PA and PB from external point P; C on the minor arc AB">
   <circle cx="150" cy="120" r="60" fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.6"/>
   <g stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.6"><line x1="300" y1="120" x2="174" y2="65"/><line x1="300" y1="120" x2="174" y2="175"/><line x1="174" y1="65" x2="210" y2="120"/><line x1="174" y1="175" x2="210" y2="120"/></g>
   <g stroke="#777" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="4 3"><line x1="150" y1="120" x2="174" y2="65"/><line x1="150" y1="120" x2="174" y2="175"/></g>
   <path d="M 276 109.5 A 26 26 0 0 0 276 130.5" fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.3"/>
   <g fill="#111"><circle cx="150" cy="120" r="2.4"/><circle cx="174" cy="65" r="2.4"/><circle cx="174" cy="175" r="2.4"/><circle cx="210" cy="120" r="2.4"/><circle cx="300" cy="120" r="2.4"/></g>
   <g font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic" font-size="15" fill="#111"><text x="138" y="112">O</text><text x="170" y="56">A</text><text x="170" y="194">B</text><text x="196" y="112">C</text><text x="306" y="125">P</text></g>
   <text x="252" y="124" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#111"><tspan font-style="italic">2θ</tspan></text></svg>
questions.solution_html:
Radius meets tangent at 90°, so in quadrilateral OAPB the angles at A and B are right angles. Hence angle AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 2θ = 180° − 2θ.

C is on the minor arc, so the arc AB that does not contain C is the major arc, subtending the reflex angle 360° − (180° − 2θ) = 180° + 2θ at the centre.

Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference: angle ACB = ½(180° + 2θ) = 90° + θ.

Equivalent route: a point D on the major arc would see angle ADB = 90° − θ, and ACBD is cyclic, so angle ACB = 180° − (90° − θ).

traps.A: θ is half the angle at P; it is not an inscribed angle here.
traps.B: 90° − θ is the angle at a point on the major arc. C is on the minor arc.
traps.D: 180° − 2θ is angle AOB, the angle at the centre.
traps.E: 180° − θ comes from subtracting θ instead of 90° − θ in the cyclic-quadrilateral route.
traps.F: 2θ is angle APB.

questions.stem_html:
The graph of y = f(x) is translated by the vector 2−3 and the resulting graph is then reflected in the y-axis.

The equation of the final graph is
questions.solution_html:
Translation by (2, −3): y = f(x − 2) − 3.

Reflection in the y-axis replaces x with −x everywhere it appears: y = f(−x − 2) − 3, i.e. y = f(−x − 2) − 3.

Order matters. Reflecting first and then translating would give f(−(x − 2)) − 3 = f(−x + 2) − 3, which is option A. The question says translate, then reflect.

traps.A: This is reflect-then-translate. The operations do not commute.
traps.C: Vertical sign wrong: the translation is −3 in y and reflection in the y-axis does not change y.
traps.D: A reflection in the x-axis, not the y-axis.
traps.E: Both the horizontal order and the vertical sign are wrong.
traps.F: Reflection in the x-axis with the translation direction reversed.

questions.stem_html:
How many real solutions does the equation

|x2 − 4| = x + 2

have?
questions.solution_html:
Case 1: x2 − 4 = x + 2, so x2 − x − 6 = 0, (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, x = 3 or −2.

Case 2: −(x2 − 4) = x + 2, so x2 + x − 2 = 0, (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0, x = −2 or 1.

Every candidate must also satisfy x + 2 ≥ 0 (a modulus is never negative): 3, −2 and 1 all pass.

The value −2 appears in both cases but is one solution. Distinct solutions: −2, 1, 3. That is 3.

Graphically: y = |x² − 4| is a W-shape touching the axis at ±2; the line y = x + 2 passes through (−2, 0), the left vertex, and cuts the curve twice more.

traps.A: 0 comes from wrongly rejecting everything through the x + 2 ≥ 0 check.
traps.B: 1 comes from only considering the case where x² − 4 ≥ 0 and rejecting −2.
traps.C: 2 comes from taking only one case.
traps.E: 4 double-counts x = −2, which arises from both cases.
traps.F: Not an identity.

questions.stem_html:
OABC is a parallelogram with OA = a and OC = c. The point N lies on OC with ON : NC = 1 : 3.

The line AN meets the diagonal OB at Y.

What is the ratio OY : YB?
questions.diagram_svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" width="330" role="img" aria-label="Parallelogram OABC with N on OC and line AN meeting diagonal OB at Y">
   <polygon points="40,160 200,160 250,60 90,60" fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.6"/>
   <line x1="40" y1="160" x2="250" y2="60" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.4"/>
   <line x1="200" y1="160" x2="52.5" y2="135" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.4"/>
   <g fill="#111"><circle cx="52.5" cy="135" r="2.6"/><circle cx="82" cy="140" r="2.6"/></g>
   <g font-family="Georgia,serif" font-style="italic" font-size="15" fill="#111"><text x="26" y="176">O</text><text x="198" y="178">A</text><text x="254" y="58">B</text><text x="80" y="54">C</text><text x="36" y="132">N</text><text x="86" y="132">Y</text></g></svg>
questions.solution_html:
ON = ¼c, and OB = a + c.

A point on AN: a + u(¼c − a) = (1 − u)a + ¼uc.

A point on OB: v(a + c) = va + vc.

Since a and c are not parallel, equate coefficients: v = 1 − u and v = ¼u. So 1 − u = ¼u, u = ⅘, v = ⅕.

OY = ⅕OB, so OY : YB = 1 : 4.

traps.A: 1 : 3 copies the given ratio ON : NC; it is not the same ratio.
traps.C: 1 : 5 comes from reading v = ⅕ as OY : YB = 1 : 5 instead of OY : OB = 1 : 5.
traps.E: 3 : 4 comes from confusing u = ⅘ (position along AN) with the position along OB.
traps.F: 4 : 1 is the answer reversed.

questions.stem_html:
A bag contains n red counters and 3 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement.

The probability that the two counters are the same colour is exactly ½.

What is the sum of all possible values of n?
questions.solution_html:
P(both red) + P(both blue) = n(n − 1)(n + 3)(n + 2) + 3 × 2(n + 3)(n + 2) = ½.

So 2n2 − 2n + 12 = n2 + 5n + 6, i.e. n2 − 7n + 6 = 0, i.e. (n − 1)(n − 6) = 0.

Check n = 1: P(RR) = 0, P(BB) = 6/12 = ½. ✓   Check n = 6: (30 + 6)/72 = ½. ✓

Both are valid, so the sum is 1 + 6 = 7.

The trap is discarding n = 1 because 'you can't pick two reds'. You can't, and that is fine: P(RR) = 0 and the blue pair alone gives ½.

traps.A: 1 is one of the values only.
traps.B: 5 comes from a slip in the quadratic (n² − 6n + 5).
traps.C: 6 is one of the values only; n = 1 also works.
traps.E: 12 comes from n² − 7n + 12 = 0 (roots 3 and 4), i.e. a wrong constant term.
traps.F: 13 comes from a doubling error in the quadratic's linear term.

questions.topic: Integer solutions of a quadratic with a parameter
questions.stem_html:
For how many integer values of k does the equation

x2 + kx + k + 3 = 0

have integer solutions?
questions.solution_html:
Let the integer roots be p and q. Then p + q = −k and pq = k + 3.

Eliminate k: pq + p + q = 3, so (p + 1)(q + 1) = 4.

Integer factor pairs of 4: (1, 4), (2, 2), (4, 1), (−1, −4), (−2, −2), (−4, −1).

So (p, q) = (0, 3), (1, 1), (3, 0), (−2, −5), (−3, −3), (−5, −2), giving k = −(p + q) = −3, −2, −3, 7, 6, 7.

Distinct values: −3, −2, 6, 7. That is 4.

Check: k = −2 gives x2 − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)2; k = 7 gives x2 + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5). ✓

Repeated roots (k = −2 and k = 6) still count: the equation has integer solutions.

traps.A: 2 comes from only using the positive factor pairs and forgetting that repeated roots count, or from discarding negatives.
traps.B: 3 comes from using the positive factor pairs only (giving k = −3, −2).
traps.D: 5 comes from counting the ordered pairs without removing duplicates but discarding one.
traps.E: 6 counts the six ordered factor pairs without noticing that (0, 3) and (3, 0) give the same k, as do (−2, −5) and (−5, −2).
traps.F: The discriminant k² − 4k − 12 must be a perfect square, which happens only finitely often.
